title: Can China Help Make Peace Between Iran and the U.S.?
summary:
Imagine two friends who are fighting, and a third friend offers to help them make up. That's kind of what's happening with China, Iran and the United States. On Wednesday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is expected in Beijing to meet his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi. It's his second trip to China since the U.S.-Israel war on Iran began at the end of February.

The visit comes just before a planned meeting between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later in September. China has been trying to look like a neutral party that wants the fighting to stop. At a BRICS summit in New Delhi this week, Xi urged countries to act as peacemakers in the Middle East. He also promoted a four-point plan: peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, following international law, and balancing development and security.

But some experts are skeptical. Hamed Vafaei, a China researcher at the University of Tehran, said seeing Xi's words as an offer to mediate between Iran and the U.S. is more of a "free interpretation" than reality. China has traditionally avoided getting deeply involved in other countries' conflicts.

Araghchi is also expected to discuss Iran's nuclear program. Last week, the U.S. and European allies pushed the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA, to refer Iran to the UN Security Council. The last such referral was 20 years ago and led to tough sanctions. This time, the move is expected to be mostly symbolic because China and Russia can veto any new Security Council measures. The U.S. has also launched "Operation Economic Outcast" to isolate Iran further.
why_it_matters: When big countries argue, prices for things like gas and food can go up everywhere, so talks like these can end up affecting your family's weekly shopping bill.

background_read: China, Iran and the United States are three powerful countries that often disagree, and China has recently tried to look like a friend to both sides.

This week's meetings are part of BRICS (a group of big developing countries — Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — that meet to work together), while the IAEA (the International Atomic Energy Agency, a United Nations group that checks what countries are doing with nuclear energy) has inspected Iran's nuclear sites for years.

In 2023 China helped Saudi Arabia and Iran agree to talk to each other again, and the UN Security Council (the part of the UN that can order punishments like sanctions) has five permanent members — the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France — and each one can veto a decision.
Article_Structure: WHO: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi, Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump, and Iran expert Hamed Vafaei of the University of Tehran.
WHAT: Araghchi is visiting Beijing to talk about peace and Iran's nuclear program, while China says it wants to act as a peacemaker in the Middle East.
WHERE: Beijing, China — plus the BRICS summit in New Delhi, India, and a planned Trump–Xi meeting in Washington later in September.
WHY: Experts doubt China will truly mediate, and a possible referral of Iran to the UN Security Council could bring back the threat of tough sanctions from 20 years ago.

perspectives.description: They say China is a neutral friend that wants the fighting to stop and is offering a peaceful four-point plan.
Researchers like Hamed Vafaei say China usually stays out of other countries' wars, so calling this a real offer to mediate is wishful thinking.
It wants a powerful friend like China to help ease the pressure coming from the United States and Europe.
